title: Own Your Trunk
subtitle: Oakland, Compton, Inglewood and Las Vegas
focus: Bay Area funk and the independent hustle, Compton lot parties, lowriders and G-funk, 1980s arena R&B, and the Las Vegas showroom tradition

intro.sub: Miami to Oakland, the long way round

intro.t: Twenty-nine hundred miles is a lot of road for not answering a question. Florida. Louisiana again. Texas, which goes on longer than some of my remixes.
Lantern's folder rides in the back with Tuesday and the Evidence Box. Ruth has the front seat. Cross has one headphone cup on and the other ear on everybody.
I'm just saying. Biggest stage in the world, and the woman is handing it to us. You don't turn down a pulpit because you don't care for the preacher.
It's a trap. It's a very nicely printed trap. Page twelve says 'exclusive'. Page nineteen says 'exclusive' again, in case we missed it.
Listen. I been on both sides of a deal. Both sides felt like a good idea at the time.
Everybody looks at the phone on the dashboard. Nobody picks it up. Not on a weekday. Not about this.
Somewhere in Arizona the van's thermometer says one hundred and eleven. Cross says 'Faith is free' and turns off the air to save the engine.
Then the Pacific, and the argument still hasn't stopped. It has only changed lanes.

outro.t: The Choir goes into Lady Whitewall's lot under a fitted cover, nose out, between two cars worth more than the building. Nobody is going to scratch that paint. Everybody in Compton knows whose mother gets called.
Then the airport at five in the morning, the tour's charter on the board, and four people who have never once flown anywhere together.
Passports. I have mine. I have yours, cousin. I have Uncle Cross's, which had expired, which I renewed, which you're welcome.
Miss Ruth, do you have a -
Ruth produces a small booklet from her handbag, the edges gone soft as cloth, the pages so stamped they look embroidered.
Nineteen sixty-four. Gospel caravan. Eleven countries on a bus with no heat. I had a passport before they did.
This other one's the new one. The old one's for showing off.
A hundred-some days to Watch Night, and I am the opening act for my own funeral.

gigs.title: Own Your Trunk
gigs.blurb: Trunk Ellis never had a hit and never had a boss. He thinks you should think about that before you sign anything.

vibe.label: Bay Area funk and independent rap

challenge.text: Never had a boss: 90% on every song, with nobody covering for you.

before.t: Oakland. The old theater's sign lit up against a September sky, every letter its own color. In the lot underneath it, a man is selling CDs out of the trunk of a Buick.
Biggest microphone in the world, baby. Five names said into it. That's all I want before I die, and I would like to not die first.
And when we're on their stage, under their lights, in their contract, who decides what gets said into it? Not us.
I'm undecided. I'm loud about it, but I'm undecided.
It's Sunday. We call Nana.
Nine o'clock in Harlem, six in Oakland. The phone on the dashboard, on speaker. She picks up on the second ring.
Nana. Lantern wants us to open their tour. Every date, all the way to Midtown on Watch Night. What do we do?
She says nothing at all. So I count it. I know how to count this. One. Two. Three. Four.
Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Eleven.
Eleven seconds of Odessa Fontaine not saying a word. It is the longest I have ever been. Then the line goes quiet in a different way.
That was a no.
That was not a no. I knew that woman when she was nineteen. That was 'decide it yourselves'.
Y'all done? Because I got a trunk full of independent music and one more hour of light.
Trunk Ellis. Porkpie hat, a cash box, a hand-lettered sign taped to the bumper: NO SINGLES. NO BOSSES. CDS $10.
I got a cousin in Oakland. Probably bought something out of your trunk.
Everybody's cousin bought something out of my trunk. That's the business model. Go play. I'll be right here. I'm always right here.

afterWin.t: After your set, Trunk Ellis is leaning on his Buick with his arms folded, which in Oakland counts as applause.
Forty years in this lot. Never had a hit. Never had a boss.
People ask which one I'd trade for the other. Neither. A hit is one summer. A boss is forever.
Lantern offered us a tour.
Course they did. So ask them the only question. When the lights go off, who owns the tape?
Whoever holds the masters holds the story. Everybody else is just in it.
The masters. The recordings themselves. Noted. Underlined. Twice.
He sells you one CD for a dollar, and he will not take the dollar until you sign a receipt. Carbon copy. One for him, one for you.
That ain't for the dollar. That's so you remember what it feels like to sign something you read.
Tuesday staples the receipt to the front of Lantern's folder, where nobody can open the folder without seeing it first.

afterLose.t: Back in the trunk, back on the road. Again.
Nobody in this lot ever got it right the first time. That's why they own it. Run it back.

gigs.title: Lot Party
gigs.blurb: Chrome, a talkbox and a women's lowrider club that will call your mother if you scratch the paint.

vibe.label: G-funk, West Coast rap and lowrider soul

challenge.text: Candy paint: earn a gold star on one song.

before.t: Compton. A swap-meet lot on a Saturday, cleared for a party. Lowriders parked in a half circle, chrome so bright it makes its own afternoon, and one car at a time rising on its hydraulics like it's been called on.
Who parked a church van next to my baby?
Lady Whitewall. President of the Whitewall Ladies Car Club. Pearl-white Impala, matching nails, a clipboard for the parking.
Scratch my paint and I call your mother.
You don't know our mother.
I will by tonight.
Oh, I like her.
On the stage, between two speaker stacks, a talkbox: a little amp, a plastic tube, a keyboard. It makes an instrument sound like a man trying to say something he can't quite get out.
Fun fact - the talkbox sends the sound up a tube into the player's mouth, and the mouth shapes it into -
Nobody stops her. She waits for it anyway.
...Uncle Cross? This is the part where you say 'not now'.
He doesn't. He has been quiet all afternoon, which for Cross is a medical event.
Pocket. After your set, I need the mic. Just for a minute.
You okay?
No. Go play.

afterWin.t: When your set ends, the hydraulics go up all around the lot, every car at once. A whole parking lot on its feet.
Cross takes the lot mic. He holds it the way he holds a record he loves: by the edges.
Listen. 1986. 'Lamppost Power', Cross Braithwaite and the Concourse Crew. Some of y'all's mamas danced to it in this lot.
That record stands on four bars I didn't play. Five people played them. I never asked their names. I been owing ever since.
So here it is. Every dollar that record ever paid me, '86 to now. I'm posting the whole accounting right here, and when I know where to send it, every dollar goes to the five.

On his phone, a spreadsheet: forty-one years of royalty statements, typed in with two fingers over a lot of motel nights. He presses post. The first DJ to pay. I have waited a long time to hear somebody say 'owing' out loud.
We didn't steal the funk. We kept it warm. But warm ain't the same as paid.
Uncle Cross...
Don't. I'll cry on that Impala and she'll call my mother.
Y'all taking that tour? Then the Choir stays here, in my lot, till you're back. Nobody touches it. Not even me.

afterLose.t: Didn't scratch a thing. Come around again.
Every car in this lot got rebuilt at least twice. Run it back.

gigs.title: The Audition
gigs.blurb: An empty arena, one spotlight, and The Birthrights watching from the good seats. Win the slot.

challenge.text: Win the slot outright: five stars on every song.

before.t: The vote happens in the van, in Lady Whitewall's lot, with the windows down. Ruth calls it. Ruth counts it. Ruth wins it.
We audition. We read every page. We sign nothing we haven't read.
Then I'm coming as opposition counsel. Somebody in this van has to object.
Inglewood. An arena built for eighteen thousand, with nobody in it. One spotlight. The seats go up into the dark like a choir loft with no choir.
Row ten, center: The Birthrights in matching jackets, and Kingston Lark with one in-ear monitor in, the way other people wear a watch.
Three songs. The panel will confer afterwards. Please don't address the panel.
Hi, Kingston.
{band}. You'll have the spotlight and house sound. The opening slot is timed to the second, every night. Please keep to time.
Try not to be memorable.
Baby, I've been trying not to be memorable for sixty years. Didn't take.
Objection.
This isn't a court.
Not yet.
The spotlight finds you. It is very bright and very lonely and it does not care whose grandchild you are.

afterWin.t: Eighteen thousand empty seats do not clap. The Birthrights do, before they can stop themselves. Then one of them looks at Kingston, and stops.
That wasn't on any click I know.
It wasn't on a click.
...Yes. I noticed.
He touches his in-ear, as if to check it is still there.
Congratulations. The slot is yours, pending signature. Miss Lark would like it signed in Las Vegas, in the Empress's room, so the family can be there.
Whose family?
The house's.
Vegas. Last time I played Vegas they made me come in through the kitchen. I'll be using the front door this time.
I got a cousin in Vegas.
You said Oakland.
I'm a man of many cousins.

afterLose.t: Again, from the top. That's what I would do.
He means it kindly. I think. The spotlight is still on. Run it back.

gigs.title: Two Shows Nightly
gigs.blurb: Sit in with the Empress, Lantern's biggest star since 1971. Then sign, or don't.

vibe.label: Showroom soul, disco and diva pop

challenge.text: Showroom standard: everyone plays on Hard or above.

before.t: Las Vegas. Behind the residency room, a dressing room with mirrors on every wall, so the Empress is never once alone in it.
Come in, darlings, come in. Mind the feathers. They bite.
Saturday Ruth. Look at you. Still on Beale?
Every Saturday. You still thirty-nine?
Darling, I have been thirty-nine for four decades. I know something about maintaining a story.
Miss St. James. Did you know? About the five?
The Empress does not turn around. She answers the mirror.
I signed with Lantern in 1971. Gus Lark told me himself, over dinner, the way a man shows you a scar. I've known ever since.
I chose my career, darling. I have loved every minute and I have slept fine. Mostly.
Why tell us now?
Because tonight you sign with his granddaughter. And she doesn't buy her enemies. She books them.
She fans herself once, which means the subject is closed. A knock: a woman in red frames, a garment bag over one arm and a travel mug in the other hand.
Good evening. I'm told my clients are signing something tonight. My clients sign nothing I haven't read. Reading is four hundred an hour. Being right is included.
Fun fact -
Tuesday. Not now. Fun facts are billed at the full rate.
Darlings. You're sitting in with me first. Two shows. The second one's the one that counts.

afterWin.t: After the second show, a private room behind the showroom. A long table, white flowers, and a pen laid out on a cloth like silverware.
Whitlock sets down Lantern's contract. Forty pages. Pryce takes it into the hall for nine minutes and comes back with forty-one.
Counselor. There appears to be an extra page.
There does appear to be. My clients keep the masters of every night they play. The rest is on page forty-one. Nobody reads page forty-one.
Riders for the opening act, Miss Lark. Standard.
Vivienne nods. You sign. Your own name, every page read. Tuesday watches the pen like it owes her money.
Then a man in a grey quarter-zip stands up at the end of the table, tablet in hand. He has been smiling the whole time. Nobody introduced him.
Graham Ellery, Perpetua Audio. So glad you're part of this. May I show you something? The Lark Five: Forever. They'll play the break live at Midtown, at the moment the catalogue changes hands.
On the tablet, five faces made of light turn to look at you. Nobody who made me ever had those faces. Nobody has ever had those faces.
We're not replacing the band. We're making sure the band never has to stop. The asset deserves that.
That's one asset.
So. You are the opening act for the thing you came to stop.

afterLose.t: Darling, I've done two shows a night for fifty years. The second one is always better. Again.
Las Vegas never closes. Neither do I. Run it back.

afterChallenge.t: Twelve-thirty-eight, Watch Night, 1967. One run-through, to see if it held together. The tape was not rolling. Gus would not waste a foot of it.
Dess had been told to stay quiet. She was a background singer. Background was where they had put her, all ten nights of the revue.
She stood by the organ with her hands folded, the way her mother had taught her to stand in the choir loft.
Bar one. Bar two. Bar three. Deacon's snare knocked like a door. Low walked underneath it like a man who knew the house.
In bar four she hollered five notes. She did not decide to. It came out of her the way the shout had come out of the church at midnight.
Everybody stopped. Ruth's hand came off the strings. The Professor turned all the way around on the bench.
Then all five of them were laughing, the kind you only do when you are young and it is past midnight and something has gone right by accident.
Gus's voice came through the talkback, flat, under the hiss: 'Do that again.'
